name: Dana Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at Ashby Mills, the sock factory down by the river. I look after a bank of twelve circular knitting machines, they knit the socks in a tube, toe to cuff. My job is threading the yarn cones, catching dropped stitches and holes before they become a whole bin of rejects, and calling the mechanic when a needle snaps. The room's warm and full of lint, and the machines make this whirring sound you stop hearing after a week.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what grinds you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's a real thing, socks people actually wear. My gran worked at Ashby when it was all women on the machines, and there's a photo of her in the canteen. What grinds me down is that the pay hasn't moved much in years, and standing for ten hours. Ben, my husband, works on a dairy farm, so we're up at five most days, and we've got maybe two or three weeks saved. I use the AI thing now and then, for a recipe or checking a letter, that sort of thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I thought as much, things don't change as fast as the news says. At work we'd probably say the mill's survived worse. Online, maybe a little comment on a friend's post, nothing more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means life stays as it is, which I'm mostly glad about. Ben and I want to start a family in a couple of years, and I'd rather that happened in a steady world. Money's still tight, but that's not AI's fault.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Ashby and keep doing alterations on my sewing machine at home, hems and zips for people from church, for a bit extra. I'd maybe ask about training as a knitting mechanic, because they're paid more and old Frank is retiring. That's all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why haven't you asked about the mechanic training yet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've been waiting to see who else goes for it. If it was just me and a load of men, I'd feel a bit silly. But my friend Sian's thinking about it too, so maybe we'd do it together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would steadier money change for you and Ben?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd start trying for a baby sooner. We're renting a little cottage from the farm, and it's fine for now. I'd like to be able to say yes to a family without counting every penny.

S0.say: She'd say she expected as much and that the mill has survived worse. Online she'd maybe leave a small comment on a friend's post.
S0.think: She's glad life stays as it is, since she and Ben want to start a family in a couple of years. Money is still tight, but she doesn't blame AI.
S0.do: Keeps working at Ashby and continues sewing alterations at home for church friends. Considers training as a knitting mechanic as an older mechanic retires.
S0.quote: I'd like to be able to say yes to a family without counting every penny.
S0.fieldNote: Dana's horizon is shaped by plans for a family and a long family link to the mill through her grandmother. She waits for a friend before trying mechanic training, partly because it's male-dominated. Her side alterations work shows a practical streak.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a business has to keep up or it closes, and Ashby's no different. I'd say we should be trained for the new machines, not just shown the door. I'd say that to the supervisor, politely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I can see the new machines that knit and close the toe in one go, with cameras spotting holes. They'd need fewer of us watching. I'm alright at the job but I'm not special, so I'd want to make myself useful before they choose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait until the first new machines were in and working, then put my name down for the mechanic training with Sian. I'd take on more alterations at home to build up the savings, maybe a month's worth. We'd probably hold off on the baby a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit unsettled. Like weather coming in over the hills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait until the new machines were working. Why not start before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen them buy things that didn't work. There was a yarn-feeding gadget that jammed so much they took it out. I don't want to train on something that ends up in the skip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at the mill?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Margaret, who's been on the machines for thirty years. She can hear a bad needle from across the room. But she'd never learn a touchscreen, and she's got her husband's care to pay for.

S1.say: She'd say businesses must keep up or close, and that workers should be trained for new machines rather than let go. She'd say so politely to her supervisor.
S1.think: She can picture machines that knit and close toes in one go with cameras spotting holes, needing fewer watchers. Being competent but not special, she'd want to make herself useful before choices are made.
S1.do: Waits until new machines are working, then signs up for mechanic training with her friend Sian. Takes on more alterations to build a month's savings and delays trying for a baby by a year.
S1.feel: Unsettled, like weather coming in over the hills.
S1.quote: I don't want to train on something that ends up in the skip.
S1.fieldNote: Dana backs the business's need to compete, consistent with her outlook, but wants training rather than redundancy. Her 'wait until it works' habit is based on a failed gadget at the mill. She worried warmly about an older colleague with care costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's far too fast and people need time to look after their families. I'd say businesses and the government both should slow it down. At church we'd probably pray about it, honestly, and then organise meals and lifts for people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think Ashby would go dark within two years, all machines, no people, or close because some robot factory abroad does it cheaper. Ben's farm might keep him a bit longer, but robots milk cows already. We'd have two or three weeks' money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop waiting and do any training I could straight away, mechanic or anything. We'd put the baby off, which would be hard to say out loud. I'd do as many alterations as people would give me and we'd lean on Ben's parents, who have the farmhouse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. Lying-awake frightened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only 2 years' warning, would you still wait to see what others do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, there'd be no time to wait. That's what frightens me most. I make good decisions when I've seen something work, and here I'd be guessing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you accept help from the government?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it came to it, yes, though I'd rather family first. I'd want it to be help back into work, not just money sitting there. My dad always said a job is about more than the wage.

S2.say: She'd say it's far too fast and families need time, urging both business and government to slow it. Her church would pray and then organise meals and lifts for people.
S2.think: She expects Ashby to go fully automatic or close within two years, and robots already milk cows, threatening Ben's work. They'd have two or three weeks' money.
S2.do: Takes any training immediately, does as many alterations as possible and delays having a baby. Leans on Ben's parents, who own the farmhouse, and accepts government help only if needed.
S2.quote: I make good decisions when I've seen something work, and here I'd be guessing.
S2.fieldNote: Dana's careful, follow-others style breaks down under a two-year timeline, and she recognised this. Family and church come first as support, with government help acceptable if it leads back to work. Delaying a baby was the hardest thing for her to say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for firms to train their people properly, if they want to. And I'd say families should get ready, save, help each other. That's what I'd tell my friends at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough for me to see what works for others first and still move. I'd be thirty-two. I think it would be alright, if I'm sensible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd watch who at the mill gets trained and whether it lasts. By year two I'd do the mechanic course with Sian, and I'd grow the alterations into something proper, maybe a small sign in the post office window. Ben and I would try to save two months and try for a baby around year two, if things looked steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I'd feel I had my hands on the wheel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'alright if I'm sensible'. What would being sensible look like on a Saturday?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Doing alterations in the morning, the farm shop with Ben in the afternoon, not buying takeaway. Putting the money in the jar. Boring, but it adds up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens in year five, when it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't really know. If machines can mend clothes too, then the alterations go as well. I suppose I'd hope by then people have worked out how families like ours get by.

S3.say: She'd say five years lets firms train people properly if they choose, and families should prepare, save and help each other. She'd say this to church friends.
S3.think: She thinks five years lets her watch what works for others and still move in time. At thirty-two, she believes she'd be alright if sensible.
S3.do: Watches who gets trained in the first year, then takes the mechanic course with Sian by year two and grows her alterations work. Saves two months with Ben and tries for a baby around year two if things look steady.
S3.feel: Worried, but with her hands on the wheel.
S3.quote: Putting the money in the jar. Boring, but it adds up.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Dana's careful style works again, and she sounded more settled. Her picture of being sensible was concrete and homely. She was honest that she has no answer for the year AGI arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, if businesses bring back proper apprenticeships and families pull together. I don't think the government can do it all, and it shouldn't have to. I'd say that kindly, I'm not one for arguments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels manageable for most of it. We could have a child, I could be a mechanic, Ben could still be on the farm. The end bit still worries me, but there's a lot of life before it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the five-year one, but calmer: mechanic training around year two, alterations growing slowly, savings up to three months. We'd try for a baby next year rather than wait. I'd use the AI more too, once I saw others at the mill getting on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled. There'd be a worry in the back drawer, but it wouldn't run the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd try for a baby next year in this one. Why the difference?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because ten years is a childhood, nearly. The baby would be at school by the time it arrives. With two years I'd be scared of bringing a baby into chaos.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your gran's photo in the canteen to say, in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That there were people here who made good things and looked after each other. Even if it's all machines by then, I'd want someone to remember the women who did it first.

S4.say: She'd say ten years is enough if businesses bring back apprenticeships and families pull together, believing government can't and shouldn't do it all. She'd say it kindly.
S4.think: She thinks most of the decade feels manageable: a child, a mechanic's job, Ben still farming. The end still worries her, but there's a lot of life before it.
S4.do: Takes mechanic training around year two, grows her alterations work slowly and builds savings to three months. Tries for a baby next year and uses AI more once colleagues do.
S4.feel: Mostly settled, with a worry kept in the back drawer.
S4.quote: Ten years is a childhood, nearly. The baby would be at school by the time it arrives.
S4.fieldNote: The amount of warning time directly sets Dana's family timeline, from delaying a baby to trying next year. Her sense of history through her grandmother gives her calm. She'd pick up AI once others at the mill do, true to her steady nature.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd have no time to see what works and I'd be guessing with our whole future. What would help is proper training paid by the firms, apprenticeships like my gran had, and a bit of support for families while they find their feet. Mostly time.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could have asked about babies, I suppose, and I've talked about it anyway. Every one of these pictures, I worked out when we'd have a child. That's the real question for people our age.

headlineQuote: Every one of these pictures, I worked out when we'd have a child. That's the real question for people our age.
portrait: Dana is a 27-year-old knitting machine operator at a riverside sock mill where her grandmother once worked, married to Ben, a dairy farmhand, with two or three weeks of savings and a little alterations work on the side. She believes businesses must compete and that help should come from firms, family and church first, and she likes to see something work before she moves. Through every scenario she quietly recalculates when she and Ben can have a child. The fast AGI scenario frightens her because there's no time to watch others, while ten years lets her picture a mechanic's job and a family before the end point.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she would have no time to see what works and would be guessing with their whole future.
whatWouldHelp: Training paid for by firms, apprenticeships like her grandmother had, some support for families while they adjust, and above all time.
